quoted_passages.text: French public debt was 60.5% of GDP in early 2000. By mid-2026 it was 119.0%, or €3.6 trillion. It climbed in steps, and the steps never fully came back down.

This is Maastricht gross debt: what central government, local authorities and social security funds owe, at face value, as a share of a year's GDP. The deficit is the yearly gap between what they spend and what they collect. Each deficit adds to the debt. The ratio falls only when the economy's cash value grows faster than the debt.

France has spent more than it collected in every year since at least 1995, where the series starts. The smallest gap was 1.3% of GDP, in 2000. Leave interest aside and France last ran a surplus in 2001, at 1.7% of GDP. It has run a deficit before interest every year since.

lede_comparison.description: Debt 119.0% of GDP in mid-2026 versus 60.5% in 2000, including 2009 and 2020 jumps and a further 14.1-point climb in the 2010s.

quoted_passages.text: French public debt reached 119.0% of GDP in mid-2026, about €3.6 trillion. In 2000 it was 60.5%. It jumped by 14.3 points in 2009 and by 16.7 points in 2020, and neither jump was undone. Between them, through the 2010s, it climbed another 14.1 points. After 2020 it dipped to 109.5% at the end of 2023, then rose again.
